rationale: A wins because it keeps the story shapes tight and the proof burden honest. "Airbnb wants the corporate travel budget, and it's routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp" turns a feature list into a real managed-travel channel story; B's "Airbnb wants corporate travel managers to stop chasing employees for receipts" is useful, but it invents a pain scene the update doesn't actually give us. B has good bones, but A is the cleaner strategist: fewer decorative inferences, sharper beats, better kill criteria.
gaps_in_A: "it won't size" overstates the facts. The update says "off a small base"; it does not say Airbnb refused to disclose the base.
"mini-hotels" is a good phrase, but "pushes Airbnb supply further toward professional operators" needs host-economics proof before it becomes more than smart inference.

A largely collapses the travel-manager operations story into the competitive Concur/Ramp channel story; there may be a separate procurement/T&E angle in the dashboard and consolidated billing pain point.
gaps_in_B: "stop chasing employees for receipts" is plausible, but invented. The update says central dashboard, consolidated billing, and Concur/Ramp integration; it does not say receipt chasing is the current pain.

"the exact infrastructure ... that hotel chains have used to lock in corporate travel budgets" overclaims. The facts do not establish hotel contracting mechanics or that Airbnb is matching them exactly.
"future of corporate travel policy" is mushy beat packaging. The 71% angle should be a skeptical data/markets story, not a fog machine.
"higher-value guest segment" implies business travelers spend more or pay higher rates. No rate, spend, or margin data was supplied.
